title: How People Analytics Is Evolving Beyond Traditional Reporting
author: Bhoomi Oza
content:
For a long time, people analytics was largely about reporting numbers. How many employees were hired? How many left? What does headcount look like across departments? These are still important questions, but the field has come a long way. Today, organizations are increasingly looking beyond what has already happened and using data to understand what might happen next.

One of the more interesting developments is the growing use of predictive analytics. Rather than waiting until employee turnover becomes a noticeable problem, HR teams can examine trends in tenure, engagement, and internal mobility to identify potential risks early on. The idea isn't to predict exactly who might leave or make assumptions about individual employees. It's to recognize broader patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed and give HR leaders an opportunity to address underlying issues before they become more serious.

Another change I've noticed is the increasing emphasis on self-service analytics. Traditionally, HR teams have relied on analysts to pull reports or answer specific data requests. With accessible dashboards and reporting tools, managers can now find much of this information themselves. This not only makes information more readily available but also allows analysts to focus on work that requires deeper investigation and interpretation. During my internship at CooperVision, I worked on a Tiers of Service framework designed to bring more structure to how HR requests are managed. That experience helped me understand how improving everyday processes can reduce repetitive work and create more room for meaningful analysis.

Technology has also played an important role in making these changes possible. Tools such as Tableau, Python, and SQL have made it easier to work with large datasets, connect information from different systems, and automate reporting processes. What I find particularly valuable is that these tools allow analysts to spend less time preparing data and more time understanding what it actually tells us. After all, having access to more data doesn't necessarily mean having better insights. The real value comes from asking the right questions and interpreting the results in a way that supports decisions.

Of course, with greater access to employee data comes greater responsibility. People analytics deals with information that can be highly personal, which makes privacy, transparency, and responsible interpretation especially important. Predictive models are useful, but they aren't always right, and their findings shouldn't be treated as definitive conclusions. HR decisions involve people, and there are often circumstances that numbers alone cannot fully explain.

What excites me most about this field is the opportunity to connect analytical thinking with real workplace challenges. As I continue gaining experience in people analytics, I'm realizing that the most valuable insights aren't necessarily the most complex ones. Sometimes, it's simply about identifying a problem early, understanding what's driving it, and helping a team make a more informed decision.

title: From Reports to Decisions: Lessons from My MS in Business Analytics
author: Bhoomi Oza
content:
When I began my Master's in Business Analytics at Santa Clara University, my primary focus was on strengthening my technical skills and developing proficiency in analytical tools. As I progressed through the program, I began to appreciate a broader aspect of analytics: its ability to translate complex information into meaningful business decisions.

One of the most valuable lessons from my coursework has been understanding the distinction between reporting data and interpreting it. While reports provide visibility into past performance, effective analysis goes further by identifying underlying patterns, evaluating potential outcomes, and informing future decisions. This perspective has shaped how I approach analytical problems, encouraging me to consider the business context before selecting the methods or tools.

My internship with the Global People Services team at CooperVision has provided an opportunity to apply this thinking in a professional setting. While developing a Tiers of Service framework to streamline HR requests, I gained a deeper understanding of how structured processes can improve operational efficiency and allow teams to dedicate more time to higher-value analytical work. The experience reinforced that meaningful improvements often begin with a clear understanding of existing challenges rather than the complexity of the solution itself.

My academic projects have further strengthened this perspective. In a machine learning project focused on sales forecasting, I examined how factors such as pricing, promotions, and advertising influenced sales performance. Beyond developing the predictive model, the experience emphasized the importance of interpreting results in a way that supports practical business decisions.

Combining graduate coursework with professional experience has been particularly valuable. While academic learning has strengthened my analytical foundation, applying these concepts in the workplace has helped me appreciate the importance of stakeholder needs, operational constraints, and clear communication.

As I approach the completion of my degree, my understanding of business analytics continues to evolve. The true measure of effective analytics lies not simply in the accuracy of its results, but in its ability to provide clarity, guide decisions, and create measurable value. This is the perspective I hope to carry forward throughout my professional career.
